prerequisites: General and Inorganic Chemistry and General and Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory exams must be passed.
To take the exam, General and Inorganic Chemistry, General and Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory, and Mathematics 1 exams must be passed.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge and understanding: The Inorganic Chemistry course aims to deepen inorganic chemistry concepts and provide basic knowledge on the chemistry of main group elements using notions of chemical bonding.

Ability to apply knowledge and understanding: The student must demonstrate the ability to correctly use all received information. The inorganic chemistry laboratory will allow verification and confirmation of inorganic chemistry concepts provided in the frontal teaching part.
Autonomy of judgment: A critical study, based on reasoning and comparison of reference bibliographic sources, compared to a merely factual study will be evaluated very positively.
Communication skills: The student must be capable of clear exposition and appropriate language in discussing the topics covered in the course.

Learning abilities: Learning abilities are highly subjective and require different times for each student; at the end of the course, the acquired notions will constitute a personal heritage on which to build subsequent professional training. Laboratory practice will serve as support and verification of the theoretical topics covered.

syllabus_topics: Structure of the nucleus. Balancing nuclear reactions. Nucleosynthesis. Mass defect. Fusion and fission. Nuclide chart. Emission spectra and electronic structure. Wave-particle duality. Wave equation. Spin multiplicity. Correlation and interelectronic repulsion. Shielding and effective nuclear charge. He and Li atoms. Periodicity of ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity. Electronegativity scales. Oxidation number. Electric dipole moment. Polarizability.
Orbital and Born-Oppenheimer approximation. LCAO-MO. Molecular Orbital diagrams for mono- and heteronuclear diatomic molecules/ions. Hypervalency. 3c-4e and 3c-2e bonding models.

Crystals. Unit cell. Crystalline systems. Close-packed and non-close-packed atom arrangements. Interstices. Metallic and intermetallic solids. Substitutional and interstitial alloys. Binary and ternary ionic solids. Geometric factors. Structure maps. Lattice enthalpy. Stability of carbonates, salts of metal ions in high oxidation states, polyinterhalides. Solubility and hydration. Solubility of alkaline earth hydroxides and sulfates.

Protonic affinity, effective protonic affinity, solvation. Solvent leveling effect. Brønsted acids: aquoacids, hydroxyacids, oxoacids. Periodic trends and substituent effects in aquoacids. Pauling's rules. Acidic, basic, amphoteric anhydrous oxides. Polyoxides and polyoxoanions. Non-aqueous solvents. Lewis acids of groups 1, 2, 13-17. HSAB theory. Superacids and superbases.

Properties of MT ions. Ligands and complexes. Oxidation state. Coordination number. Denticity. Electronic classification of ligands. Nomenclature of coordination compounds. Coordination geometries and geometric isomerism. Fluxionality. Optical isomerism. Polymetallic complexes. Complex formation constants. Chelate effect and macrocyclic effect.
Crystal Field Theory (CFT). Spectrochemical series and color. High and low spin.

Optical spectroscopic methods in inorganic chemistry. Electronic, vibrational, rotational spectroscopy. Notes on absorption and emission spectroscopy, Lambert-Beer law, electronic absorption spectra of molecular halogens.

Laboratory prevention and safety: regulations, PPE and EPC. Experimental data treatment. Rules of conduct. Storage of reagents and solvents. Waste disposal. Prohibition, prescription, rescue signs. Labeling. Risk phrases. Classification of fires and fire extinguishing methods. Laboratory experiments: 1) copper reaction cycle; 2) dry assays; 3) periodic properties of groups II and VII; 4) synthesis and analysis of ammonium decavanadate hexahydrate; 5) introduction to coordination chemistry; 6) UV-Vis electronic absorption spectroscopy on molecular halogens.
assessment_rules: The assessment includes a single oral exam. The score is expressed out of thirty and derives from the evaluation of the oral exam, taking into account the work done individually or in groups in the laboratory. Conceptual rigor, correctness of logical procedures, adequacy of the proposed solution, and use of appropriate language are considered. Satisfying the theoretical foundations of the experiments, assessed through personal assignments for each experiment, and a positive evaluation of laboratory practice are necessary conditions for a passing grade. Higher grades are awarded to students whose work meets all four aspects. To achieve 30/30 cum laude, the student must demonstrate excellent knowledge of every topic covered.
